terms.gloss: five past one, and so on: the hour, then cum and the twelfths of the hour
evidence: Andresian p. 49: hōra nōna cum quadrante
M-O s.v. o’clock, after Egger: est hōra septima cum quadrante
terms.comment: Each twelfth of the hour (ūncia hōrae) is five minutes, and the hour takes them with cum and the ablative: :05 cum ūnciā · :10 cum sextante · :15 cum quadrante · :20 cum triente · :25 cum quīncūnce · :30 cum sēmisse · :35 cum septūnce · :40 cum besse · :45 cum dōdrante · :50 cum dēxtante · :55 cum deūnce. The hour is the ordinal (prīma … duodecima); “at” a time puts the hour in the ablative: hōrā octāvā cum sextante, at ten past eight.

terms.gloss: a quarter past one, with et
terms.comment: Traupman gives the quarter-hours this way: prīma hōra et quadrāns, et sēmihōra, et dōdrāns; “at” hōrā septimā et quadrante.

phrases.latin: longissimus diēs est aequinoctiālium hōrārum XIIII atque dīmidiae cum trīcēsimā ūnius hōrae
phrases.english: the longest day is fourteen and a half equinoctial hours, with a thirtieth of an hour
We’ll have dinner at twenty to seven.

history.html: The twelfths are used of the hour in Pliny, as lengths of time rather than readings of a clock: the moon shines longer each day by dōdrantēs sēmunciās hōrārum (NH 2.58); the stars are not seen until a dōdrāns hōrae before sunrise (18.219); the moon gains a dēxtāns hōrae and a sīcīlicus a night (18.324). Elsewhere he gives fractions of the hour in the Greek way (bis quīnta pars, tertiae duae, 6.213–218), and once joins one to the hours with cum (6.214). Telling the clock time by the quarter-hour is modern Latin: Traupman 81 with et; Egger (quoted in M-O s.v. o’clock) and Andresian p. 49 with cum. Every twelfth, in steps of five minutes, is current spoken Latin (see the sources).
